what: The qualitative findings of the 2026-09-09 audit of OpenAI's Navier–Stokes claim, as records the report reads: the statement-fidelity rows (Clay ↔ Formal Conjectures ↔ Mathlib), the paper-versus-Lean alignment, the weak points of the writeup ranked, and what was verified by hand. Every count on the page comes from lean-repo.json, probes.json and build.json, never from here.

sources.memos: five section memos (§3+§10, §4+App B, §5+App A, §6+§7, §8+§9+App C) and one Lean map, written 2026-09-09 by six independent readers; consolidated in dissection.md

claim.theorem: For every ν > 0 there exist a force f ∈ C_c^∞(R³×(0,∞)), a compact K, and smooth (u,p) on R³×[0,1) supported in K, solving Navier–Stokes from rest, with sup_{t<1} ‖u(t)‖_{L²} < ∞ and lim sup_{t↑1} ‖u(t)‖_{L^∞} = ∞; consequently no smooth global solution with uniformly bounded energy exists — Clay alternative (C). Corollary 10.6: alternative (D) on the torus.
claim.mechanism: A self-similar axisymmetric core (ℓr ≍ τ^{1/2}, ℓz ≍ τ^{1/2−h}, |uθ|,|uz| ≍ τ^{−1/2−h}, |ur| = O(τ^{−1/2}), 0 < h < 1/100) whose annular momentum residual is unbounded, cancelled by the averaged Reynolds stress of two families of shear-amplified oscillatory pulses carried on an auxiliary torus, corrected at every order in q^{2h} to a flat remainder, joined to an exact radial-heat exterior and cut off; the force is defined as the residual and shown to extend smoothly through t = 1; uniqueness with no growth condition on the pressure transfers the growth to any competitor.
claim.lineage: Descends from Córdoba–Martínez-Zoroa's forced-blowup program (the paper's refs [6]–[8], arXiv:2410.22920 for IPM), with a different role for the amplified waves: they supply a mean momentum flux rather than the singular field itself.

The definitions were written by DeepMind's Formal Conjectures project on 2026-05-15 (#1457), last touched 2026-07-27, byte-identical to main on 2026-09-09; OpenAI's copy differs in imports, attributes, namespace and local notation only. The direction rule: the theorem is a negation, so a weak or junk-valued solution notion only strengthens it; a gap could hide only in a competitor class stronger than Clay's or a data hypothesis weaker than Clay's, and neither occurs.

paperVsLean.contrast: The Euler theorem in the same repository DOES carry it: Euler.exists_compact_smooth_euler_singularity (Euler/Solution.lean:43) asserts, for a nonzero compactly supported smooth datum, a solution on [0,T*) with 0 < T* ≤ 1, a uniform energy bound ∃ E, ∀ t ∈ [0,T*), ∫‖v‖² < E, maximality as an IFF (a solution on [0,T] exists iff T < T*), the C¹ norm bounded on every shorter interval, limsup of the C¹ norm = ⊤ at T*, the Beale–Kato–Majda integral = ⊤, and no global smooth finite-energy solution. Same team, same week, same repository — so the omission on the Navier–Stokes side reads as an oversight, not an obstacle.

weakPoints.what: The swirl maximum principle: the axisymmetric background alone (r·uθ = q^{−h}H, unbounded) is impossible for a forced flow from rest with bounded force; the non-axisymmetric pulses are the only reason the theorem is not false, and the paper never says so. Not a gap in the proof — the Lean candidate is whatever it is — but the single sentence a referee would demand in the introduction, and the reason h > 0 (type II) is forced rather than chosen.

Endpoint regularity of the local field up to τ = 0 for q ≥ c: one paragraph ('differentiating its fixed linear ODE gives the bounds at every derivative order'), no estimate displayed. Lemma 10.2 region (a), hence the force's smoothness at t = 1 away from the origin, rests on it.
Flatness is stated for 0 ≤ X ≤ X₁ as q ↓ 0 without explicit uniformity in η ∈ (−1,1); (10.9) needs it on a full neighbourhood of (0,1) including η → ±1. Plausible, not displayed.

Admissibility of next-cycle sources for the pulse inverse after temporal inverses that spread over the torus: 'the pulse cutoff ψ restores the fixed enlarged local torus rectangle support' is asserted. The only unstated induction hypothesis in §9.

Every constant is 'sufficiently small/large' and none is numeric: h < 1/100 is printed but Lemma 4.8 needs h < min{λ, e^{−T_d}} with T_d = e^{M_d}+10; the §6 derivative scale exceeds 1 only for dyadic level ℓ ≳ 3×10⁸; flatness to order N needs more than 1000(N+K_m) cycles; the cutoff flatness costs ~10⁷N integrations by parts. Not a gap in logic; the proof is entirely asymptotic.

The Lipschitz bounds of (Φ,u) ↦ J_νR_i on the weighted analytic space are asserted in one sentence; every constant of the inner construction descends from them; the η-analyticity radius is O(σ_*), never said.

'2 + h < a' on the terminal collar holds for Z = 2d/X ≲ 1.5 and fails for Z ≥ 3 at h = 0.01 (a = 2 + 2h + 2Z𝓗′/𝓗); it holds on the collar only because X_tail ≫ 1, a dependence that belongs in Appendix A's choice of X_tail.
Continuation to X_i = 110 is a prose sketch: unspecified interpolation lengths, 'p₁ > 2 by continuity'.

Lemma 5.1 needs the leading profile η-analytic on [0, a²] with a² > X_cut; Theorem 4.6(i) gives analyticity on [0, X_an]; that a² ≤ X_an and that the non-analytic edits (B.8 bumps, C.2/C.3 patch, A.7 patch) lie beyond X_an is never stated where needed.

The order-n coefficient equations were stated with sample terms derived (pp. 46–47). DISCHARGED by computer algebra at this build: instruments/navierstokes/probes/coefficient_equations.py substitutes (5.1) into the axisymmetric operator and recovers (5.2)–(5.6), the sparsity of A₁ in (5.7) and the divisibility of Ω_k by X exactly as printed (69 identities). Kept in the list as the record of a check, not a gap.

The zero-Haar-mean part of the pulse covariance is larger than its mean by ≍ S_*^{1/2}/(4r₀²(1+b_g²)) and is never quantified in §6–7; its cancellation is the fast-time inverse of §8.5, whose derivative cost is never tabulated against the mean route.
Class preservation of the signed-amplitude map at every cycle needs |T₀| ≥ cζ on the modulated profile; proved in Prop C.3, never cited in §9.
q_* overloaded: Lemma 9.7 chooses q_big ≤ an earlier q_*; Theorem 3.1 then defines q_* := q_big. Not circular; the reader supplies the disambiguation.

refusals: No verdict on the theorem is issued by the paper reading; the verdict is the Lean build's and the independent kernel's, recorded in build.json.
No numerical solution of the profile equations is a certification: the paper contains no numerics and none of its constants is a number.

obstructions.what: The adversarial pass: every known theorem that forbids a Navier–Stokes singularity of some kind, tested against the construction. A construction that violated one would be refuted; this one evades each, and one evasion is load-bearing and unstated.

rows.statement: for axisymmetric u the swirl Γ = r·uθ satisfies ∂ₜΓ + u_r∂_rΓ + u_z∂_zΓ = Γ_rr − Γ_r/r + Γ_zz + r·f_θ, a drift–diffusion equation with no zeroth-order term; hence sup|Γ(t)| ≤ ∫₀ᵗ sup|r f_θ| for Γ(0) = 0, so a bounded compactly supported force from rest gives a BOUNDED swirl and |uθ| ≤ C/r for all t
rows.construction: the leading field has uθ = q^{−1/2−h}E at r = √(2qX), i.e. Γ = √(2X) q^{−h} E → ∞ — the paper writes r·uθ⁽⁰⁾ = q^{−h}H itself (p. 27)
rows.verdict: the axisymmetric background ALONE is impossible as a forced flow from rest; the theorem survives only because the physical field is not axisymmetric — the pulses carry nonzero integer angular frequencies (p. 12) and their Reynolds flux breaks the maximum principle for the angular mean. Load-bearing, and nowhere stated in the paper. Derived and checked symbolically in the battery.

rows.obstruction: type-I exclusion for axisymmetric flows (Chen–Strain–Yau–Tsai 2008; Koch–Nadirashvili–Seregin–Šverák 2009)
rows.statement: an axisymmetric solution with |u| ≤ C/√(T−t) (or C/r) does not blow up; a bounded force rescales to zero, so the exclusion covers forced flows
rows.construction: |u| ≍ τ^{−1/2−h}: type II by the factor τ^{−h}; and the flow is not axisymmetric
rows.verdict: evaded twice — h > 0 is what the type-I theorems force, and the paper never says so

rows.statement: axisymmetric flows without swirl are globally regular
rows.construction: the core has swirl, injected by f_θ (the unforced flow from rest would have Γ ≡ 0 by the maximum principle)

rows.statement: a singularity at T requires ∫₀ᵀ‖u‖_∞² dt = ∞
a Leray solution has sup‖u‖₂ < ∞ and ∫‖∇u‖₂² < ∞
rows.construction: core energy τ^{1/2−3h} → 0; dissipation rate τ^{−1/2−3h}, integrable iff h < 1/6
rows.verdict: met, and h < 1/6 is a real constraint the printed h < 1/100 satisfies

rows.statement: the singular set has parabolic 1-Hausdorff measure zero; singular times have 1/2-Hausdorff measure zero

threeQuestions.q: Are the 'sufficiently small/large' parameters explicit numbers in Lean?
threeQuestions.a: No. h, N, Λ, C, q_* and the cycle schedule are all existentials or Classical.choice; the only numeric constants are κ = 10⁻⁵, Λ_chart = 4 − √2, X_big = 100, X_i = 110. Nothing in either artifact bounds h numerically.

threeQuestions.q: Is the constructed field non-axisymmetric in Lean (the pulses' nonzero angular frequency)?
threeQuestions.a: Yes, and it is proved rather than assumed: the angular mode enters at HarmonicFields.field … (kp : ℤ) (:107); the actual construction fixes angularMode l n : ℤ with the theorem angularMode_ne_zero (ActualInitialization.lean:52). There is no literal ¬Axisymmetric theorem, but the nonzero angular mode is exactly what the swirl maximum principle requires the field to have — the formal object does evade the obstruction the paper never names.

threeQuestions.q: Which theorem asserts the growth, and along what path?
threeQuestions.a: ConstructedSlowBase.origin (:892) gives u(t,0) = (1−t)^{−(1/2+h)}·j·e_z and FinalSlowBase.axis_tendsto (:373) sends it to infinity along t ↦ (t,0): the AXIAL component ON the axis. The paper's (10.20)–(10.21) uses a different path, off-axis at r = √(2X_in τ), where the AZIMUTHAL component diverges. Both give lim sup ‖u‖_∞ = ∞; the formal witness is the simpler one, and no Lean theorem bounds the swirl r·u_θ from below.

findings.energyAsymmetry: For Euler the positive content is formalized in full, energy bound included; for Navier–Stokes — the Millennium problem, and the one the announcement leads with — the energy clause is the single missing field of an otherwise complete candidate structure, and the lemma that would supply it sits unused in the same library.
